claim: Controlling the numerous joints of a prosthetic arm necessary to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects remains challenging.
source: Yet, controlling the numerous joints of a prosthetic arm necessary to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects remains challenging.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field in the abstract.

claim: An intuitive, movement-based prosthesis control was designed that leverages natural arm coordination to predict distal joints missing in people with transhumeral limb loss based on proximal residual limb motion and knowledge of the movement goal.
source: Here, we designed an intuitive, movement-based prosthesis control that leverages natural arm coordination to predict distal joints missing in people with transhumeral limb loss based on proximal residual limb motion and knowledge of the movement goal.
evidence: This describes the main contribution of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: The control was validated on 29 participants, including seven with above-elbow limb loss.
source: This control was validated on 29 participants, including seven with above-elbow limb loss, who picked and placed bottles in a wide range of locations in virtual reality, with median success rates over 99% and movement times identical to those of natural movements.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental validation conducted.

claim: Participants achieved median success rates over 99% when picking and placing bottles in virtual reality.
source: This control was validated on 29 participants, including seven with above-elbow limb loss, who picked and placed bottles in a wide range of locations in virtual reality, with median success rates over 99% and movement times identical to those of natural movements.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: Movement times with the control were identical to those of natural movements.
source: This control was validated on 29 participants, including seven with above-elbow limb loss, who picked and placed bottles in a wide range of locations in virtual reality, with median success rates over 99% and movement times identical to those of natural movements.
evidence: This is a comparative result from the experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: The control enabled 15 participants, including three with limb differences, to reach and grasp real objects with a robotic arm.
source: This control also enabled 15 participants, including three with limb differences, to reach and grasp real objects with a robotic arm operated according to the same principle.
evidence: This describes the physical proof of concept validation conducted.

claim: The control was achieved without any prior training.
source: Remarkably, this was achieved without any prior training, indicating that this control is intuitive and instantaneously usable.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: The control is intuitive and instantaneously usable.
source: Remarkably, this was achieved without any prior training, indicating that this control is intuitive and instantaneously usable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that no prior training was needed.

claim: The control could be used for phantom limb pain management in virtual reality.
source: It could be used for phantom limb pain management in virtual reality, or to augment the reaching capabilities of invasive neural interfaces usually more focused on hand and grasp control.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the control system.

claim: The control could augment the reaching capabilities of invasive neural interfaces usually more focused on hand and grasp control.
source: It could be used for phantom limb pain management in virtual reality, or to augment the reaching capabilities of invasive neural interfaces usually more focused on hand and grasp control.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the control system.

claim: Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) is a technique used in the field of bionic limbs.
source: The field of bionic limbs has seen great progress over the last few years, including Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) (Kuiken, 2009), osseointegration (Jönsson et al., 2011), chronically implanted sensors and stimulators for bidirectional communication with the nervous system (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a; D'Anna et al., 2019; Zollo et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2019), and advanced signal processing to encode and decode sensorimotor signals (Jezernik et al., 2001; Farina et al., 2023; Cracchiolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited as an existing technique in the field.

claim: Osseointegration is a technique used in the field of bionic limbs.
source: The field of bionic limbs has seen great progress over the last few years, including Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) (Kuiken, 2009), osseointegration (Jönsson et al., 2011), chronically implanted sensors and stimulators for bidirectional communication with the nervous system (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a; D'Anna et al., 2019; Zollo et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2019), and advanced signal processing to encode and decode sensorimotor signals (Jezernik et al., 2001; Farina et al., 2023; Cracchiolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited as an existing technique in the field.

claim: Chronically implanted sensors and stimulators enable bidirectional communication with the nervous system.
source: The field of bionic limbs has seen great progress over the last few years, including Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) (Kuiken, 2009), osseointegration (Jönsson et al., 2011), chronically implanted sensors and stimulators for bidirectional communication with the nervous system (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a; D'Anna et al., 2019; Zollo et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2019), and advanced signal processing to encode and decode sensorimotor signals (Jezernik et al., 2001; Farina et al., 2023; Cracchiolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited as an existing technique in the field.

claim: Simultaneous and proportional real-time myoelectric control has been achieved for two to three DoFs.
source: Indeed, although simultaneous and proportional real-time myoelectric control has been achieved for two to three DoFs (de Rugy et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2012; Hahne et al., 2015; Ameri et al., 2014; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014b; Smith et al., 2016; Nowak et al., 2022), difficulties appear (Hahne et al., 2015) and performance deteriorates as the number of DoFs increases (e.g. success rate dropped from 96 to 37% from one to three DoFs in Nowak et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited as an existing achievement in myoelectric control.

claim: Performance of myoelectric control deteriorates as the number of DoFs increases.
source: Indeed, although simultaneous and proportional real-time myoelectric control has been achieved for two to three DoFs (de Rugy et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2012; Hahne et al., 2015; Ameri et al., 2014; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014b; Smith et al., 2016; Nowak et al., 2022), difficulties appear (Hahne et al., 2015) and performance deteriorates as the number of DoFs increases (e.g. success rate dropped from 96 to 37% from one to three DoFs in Nowak et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited as a known limitation in myoelectric control.

claim: Success rate in myoelectric control dropped from 96 to 37% from one to three DoFs in Nowak et al., 2022.
source: Indeed, although simultaneous and proportional real-time myoelectric control has been achieved for two to three DoFs (de Rugy et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2012; Hahne et al., 2015; Ameri et al., 2014; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014b; Smith et al., 2016; Nowak et al., 2022), difficulties appear (Hahne et al., 2015) and performance deteriorates as the number of DoFs increases (e.g. success rate dropped from 96 to 37% from one to three DoFs in Nowak et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result cited from another study.

claim: In the case of an amputation at the humeral level, none of the forearm, wrist, and hand muscles would remain.
source: In the case of an amputation at the humeral level, none of the forearm wrist, and hand muscles would remain, and the important additional DoF of the elbow would need to be controlled.
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical consequences of transhumeral amputation.

claim: The important additional DoF of the elbow would need to be controlled in transhumeral amputation.
source: In the case of an amputation at the humeral level, none of the forearm wrist, and hand muscles would remain, and the important additional DoF of the elbow would need to be controlled.
evidence: This is a statement about control requirements for transhumeral prostheses.

claim: TMR is usually geared toward recovering forearm supination-pronation and hand opening-closing.
source: Although TMR could be used to recover valid control signals by transferring residual arm nerves controlling missing distal muscles and joints to compartments of remaining muscles (Kuiken, 2009; Kuiken et al., 2007), this is usually geared toward recovering forearm supination-pronation and hand opening-closing (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Hargrove et al., 2017), arguably more important and available in commercial prosthesis, rather than wrist DoFs (flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation) which are nevertheless critical to orient the hand in space (Montagnani et al., 2015a; Kanitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited as the typical application of TMR.

claim: Wrist DoFs (flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation) are critical to orient the hand in space.
source: Although TMR could be used to recover valid control signals by transferring residual arm nerves controlling missing distal muscles and joints to compartments of remaining muscles (Kuiken, 2009; Kuiken et al., 2007), this is usually geared toward recovering forearm supination-pronation and hand opening-closing (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Hargrove et al., 2017), arguably more important and available in commercial prosthesis, rather than wrist DoFs (flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation) which are nevertheless critical to orient the hand in space (Montagnani et al., 2015a; Kanitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited as an important functional requirement.

claim: No myoelectric solution exists to simultaneously and intuitively control the four arm DoFs (from elbow to wrist included) that are necessary for people with transhumeral limb loss.
source: In the end, no myoelectric solution exists to simultaneously and intuitively control the four arm DoFs (from elbow to wrist included) that are necessary for people with transhumeral limb loss in order to correctly position and orient their prosthetic hand to grasp objects in a large reachable space.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current technology.

claim: Control strategies exploiting natural synergies in arm coordination have already been used to predict distal joints from the motion of proximal ones.
source: Control strategies exploiting natural synergies in arm coordination (Soechting and Lacquaniti, 1981; Desmurget et al., 1995) have already been used to predict distal joints from the motion of proximal ones (Popovic and Popovic, 2001; Kaliki et al., 2013; Merad et al., 2020; Merad et al., 2018; Montagnani et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is cited as existing work in the field.

claim: Previous movement-based controls have been mostly confined to the control of one DoF.
source: However, these have been mostly confined to the control of one DoF (i.e. either the elbow [Popovic and Popovic, 2001; Merad et al., 2020; Merad et al., 2018] or the wrist supination-pronation [Montagnani et al., 2015b], reconstructed from shoulder movement), or relying on additional unnatural movements to increase functionality (Kaliki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited as a limitation of previous approaches.

claim: Adding target position and orientation to an ANN trained to predict four arm distal DoFs from proximal motion greatly improves these predictions.
source: We showed recently that adding target position and orientation to an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) trained to predict four arm distal DoFs (elbow to wrist) from proximal (shoulder) motion greatly improves these predictions, as well as human-in-the-loop control using them (Mick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Performance in Mick et al., 2021 remained lower than natural movements, with increased compensatory movements from trunk and shoulder.
source: Yet, performance remained lower than natural movements, with increased compensatory movements from trunk and shoulder, a limited workspace, and a control design not directly applicable to people with transhumeral limb loss (Mick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited as a limitation of previous work by the authors.

claim: Critical changes were brought about to overcome limitations of previous work.
source: Critical changes were brought about here to overcome all those limitations, and enabled 29 participants (including seven with transhumeral limb loss) to perform as well as natural, without any prior training, at picking and placing a bottle in a wide reachable space in virtual reality.
evidence: This describes the improvements made in the current study.

claim: 300 'plausible' target locations were determined randomly within the full range of motion established individually for each joint of each participant.
source: To maximize the workspace of this task, 300 'plausible' target locations (i.e. position and orientation) were determined randomly within the full range of motion established individually for each joint of each participant (see Figure 1a, Methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for target generation.

claim: Natural arm movements recorded to pick and place bottles at 300 targets were used to train the ANN involved in the movement-based control.
source: Natural arm movements recorded to pick and place bottles at those 300 targets were then used to train the ANN involved in our movement-based control (Figure 1c, cf next section), but also to establish a new set of 200 'possible' targets within the workspace actually covered by the participants' arm during the initial acquisition (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the training data for the ANN.

claim: A set of 200 'possible' targets was established within the workspace actually covered by the participants' arm during the initial acquisition.
source: Natural arm movements recorded to pick and place bottles at those 300 targets were then used to train the ANN involved in our movement-based control (Figure 1c, cf next section), but also to establish a new set of 200 'possible' targets within the workspace actually covered by the participants' arm during the initial acquisition (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the generation of test targets.

claim: Anatomical joints' limits are interdependent in a way that makes it uncomfortable or impossible to produce arm configurations with maximal excursion simultaneously at multiple joints.
source: Although 'plausible' targets are all supposed to be reachable, in practice, anatomical joints' limits are interdependent in a way that makes it uncomfortable or impossible to produce arm configurations with maximal excursion simultaneously at multiple joints.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the methodology.

claim: An unsupervised self-organizing neural network was used to identify 200 nodes that best represent the arm postures actually produced by participants.
source: To circumvent this, we used an unsupervised self-organizing neural network (Fritzke, 1994) to identify 200 nodes that best represent the arm postures actually produced by participants, and used forward kinematics to turn these nodes into target locations, thereby obtaining a set of 200 possible targets guaranteed to be reachable with natural arm movements (Figure 1d, see Methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology for generating possible targets.

claim: Typical movement times were approximately 1.3 s between pick and place.
source: Video 1 illustrates a participant completing the task at a comfortable yet sustained pace, representative of the overall performance observed in our experiments (i.e. with typical movement times of approximately 1.3 s between pick and place).
evidence: This is stated as a typical performance measure observed in the experiments.

claim: The ANN was trained to reconstruct five distal arm angles from shoulder kinematics plus contextual target information.
source: After being trained to reconstruct five distal arm angles from proximal shoulder kinematics plus target location (3D position and 2D orientation, see Methods), the ANN illustrated in Figure 1c was used to control a Hybrid Arm emulating the behavior of a residual upper arm fitted with a transhumeral prosthesis (Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes the ANN training approach.

claim: Shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator.
source: To this end, shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining joint angles were driven by predictions from the ANN.
evidence: This describes the control scheme for the Hybrid Arm.

claim: The five remaining joint angles of the Hybrid Arm were driven by predictions from the ANN.
source: To this end, shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the Hybrid Arm were operated from real shoulder movements produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining joint angles were driven by predictions from the ANN.
evidence: This describes the control scheme for the Hybrid Arm.

claim: The ANN could be trained either solely from the operator's own natural movements (Own ANN) or from those of multiple other participants (Generic ANN).
source: Importantly, the ANN could be trained either solely from the operator's own natural movements (Own ANN, see Methods) or from those of multiple other participants (Generic ANN).
evidence: This describes two different training approaches for the ANN.

claim: In Exp1, 10 right-handed subjects were tested on 200 possible target locations with the intuitive prosthesis control trained on their own movements.
source: After an initial acquisition in which they picked-and-placed 300 plausible targets with their right arm in a wide workspace, 10 right-handed subjects were tested on 200 possible target locations with our intuitive prosthesis control trained on their own movements (Exp1, TestOwn, Figure 3a) before being tested again on the same targets with their natural arm movements (TestNat).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, median success rate was 100% for TestNat and 99.7% for TestOwn.
source: Results indicate high success rates for both conditions (median success rate of 100% and 99.7% for TestNat and TestOwn, respectively), with a minor (<1%) albeit significant difference between them (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=1886; McNemar test, p=0.023, df = 1; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, there was a significant difference in success rate between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.023).
source: Results indicate high success rates for both conditions (median success rate of 100% and 99.7% for TestNat and TestOwn, respectively), with a minor (<1%) albeit significant difference between them (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=1886; McNemar test, p=0.023, df = 1; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, median movement times were 1.25 s for TestOwn and 1.17 s for TestNat.
source: Regarding movement times (i.e. time taken to reach and validate each target from the previous one), results were also closely similar and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 1.25 s vs 1.17 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.378, t=–0.927, df = 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, movement times were not significantly different between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.378).
source: Regarding movement times (i.e. time taken to reach and validate each target from the previous one), results were also closely similar and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 1.25 s vs 1.17 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.378, t=–0.927, df = 9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, median shoulder volume was 0.22 dm³ for TestOwn and 0.18 dm³ for TestNat.
source: The volume spread by the shoulder's trajectory throughout a phase, which includes compensatory movements of the body that might be elicited to compensate for imperfect control (see Mick et al., 2021), was also comparable and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 0.22 dm3 vs 0.18 dm3, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.058, t=–2.168, df = 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp1.

claim: In Exp1, shoulder volume was not significantly different between TestOwn and TestNat (p=0.058).
source: The volume spread by the shoulder's trajectory throughout a phase, which includes compensatory movements of the body that might be elicited to compensate for imperfect control (see Mick et al., 2021), was also comparable and not significantly different between conditions (TestOwn vs TestNat; n=10; medians of 0.22 dm3 vs 0.18 dm3, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.058, t=–2.168, df = 9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp1.

claim: The movement-based control trained on the own natural movements of each participant enabled an almost perfect success rate (99.7%).
source: Overall, our movement-based control trained on the own natural movements of each participant enabled an almost perfect success rate (99.7%), and movement times similar to that with their natural arm to pick and place the bottle in the wide workspace tested.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp1.

claim: A critical step toward building an efficient generic model for a new user was to remap hand position data from previous participants to the arm dimensions of that new user.
source: As the relationship between hand locations and arm configurations depends on segment dimensions that differ between participants, a critical step toward building an efficient generic model for a new user was to remap hand position data from previous participants to the arm dimensions of that new user (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach for the Generic ANN.

claim: Forward kinematics was used to remap data from all participants of Exp1 before using them to train the generic ANN.
source: This was done using forward kinematics to remap data from all participants of Exp1 before using them to train the generic ANN to be used for intuitive control in TestGeneric by each participant of Exp2 (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology for training the Generic ANN.

claim: In Exp2, 12 participants (six left-handed) were tested on the movement-based control using either the generic model or the model based on their own movements.
source: After an initial acquisition phase equivalent to that of Exp1, 12 participants (six left-handed) were tested on our movement-based control using either the generic model (TestGeneric) or the model based on their own movements (TestOwn).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, participants achieved median success rates of 99% or higher in all conditions.
source: Participants achieved high success rates in all conditions (median success rates of 99% or higher, Figure 3b), although minor differences between conditions (<1%) were found significant (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; n=2268; medians of 99.50% vs 99.24% vs 100%, respectively, Cochran's Q test, p=5.19.10–12, Q=51.97, df = 2; post-hoc McNemar test with Bonferroni adjustment; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=6.42.10–5, chi.sq=18.1, df = 1; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=8.58.10–3, chi.sq=8.89, df = 1; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=3.24.10–10, chi.sq=41.7, df = 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, median success rates were 99.50% for TestOwn, 99.24% for TestGeneric, and 100% for TestNat.
source: Participants achieved high success rates in all conditions (median success rates of 99% or higher, Figure 3b), although minor differences between conditions (<1%) were found significant (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; n=2268; medians of 99.50% vs 99.24% vs 100%, respectively, Cochran's Q test, p=5.19.10–12, Q=51.97, df = 2; post-hoc McNemar test with Bonferroni adjustment; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=6.42.10–5, chi.sq=18.1, df = 1; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=8.58.10–3, chi.sq=8.89, df = 1; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=3.24.10–10, chi.sq=41.7, df = 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, median movement times remained below 1.4 s in all conditions.
source: Median movement times remained below 1.4 s in all conditions (Figure 3c), with no significant difference found between conditions (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.181, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=1.848).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, there was no significant difference in movement times between conditions (p=0.181).
source: Median movement times remained below 1.4 s in all conditions (Figure 3c), with no significant difference found between conditions (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.181, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=1.848).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, median shoulder volumes were 0.23 dm³ for TestOwn, 0.43 dm³ for TestGeneric, and 0.14 dm³ for TestNat.
source: With respect to the volume spread by the shoulder during the Test phases (Figure 3d), the statistical analysis revealed a significant effect of condition, (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians of 0.23dm3 vs 0.43 dm3 vs 0.14 dm3, respectively, n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.003, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=7.806), with post-hoc tests indicating a higher volume for TestGeneric than for Test Nat (Tukey test with Bonferroni correction; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=0.385; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=0.025; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=0.347).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, there was a significant effect of condition on shoulder volume (p=0.003).
source: With respect to the volume spread by the shoulder during the Test phases (Figure 3d), the statistical analysis revealed a significant effect of condition, (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians of 0.23dm3 vs 0.43 dm3 vs 0.14 dm3, respectively, n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.003, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=7.806), with post-hoc tests indicating a higher volume for TestGeneric than for Test Nat (Tukey test with Bonferroni correction; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=0.385; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=0.025; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=0.347).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, shoulder volume for TestGeneric was significantly higher than for TestNat (p=0.025).
source: With respect to the volume spread by the shoulder during the Test phases (Figure 3d), the statistical analysis revealed a significant effect of condition, (TestOwn vs TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians of 0.23dm3 vs 0.43 dm3 vs 0.14 dm3, respectively, n=12; RM ANOVA test, p=0.003, DFn = 2, DFd = 22, F=7.806), with post-hoc tests indicating a higher volume for TestGeneric than for Test Nat (Tukey test with Bonferroni correction; TestOwn vs TestNat, p=0.385; TestGeneric vs TestNat, p=0.025; TestOwn vs TestGeneric, p=0.347).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp2.

claim: In Exp2, the spread volumes never exceeded 1 liter.
source: Despite this difference, the spread volumes remained contained, never exceeding 1 liter (Figure 3d), which appears reasonable given the high compensations that could have occurred with less efficient controls over the wide workspace spanned by the targets.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from Exp2.

claim: The control based on a generic model enabled new participants to reach almost all targets (>99%) as well as with their natural arm regardless of handedness.
source: Overall, our control based on a generic model trained on data from other participants enabled, therefore, new participants to reach almost all targets (>99%) as well as with their natural arm (or an intuitive control trained on their own natural movements) regardless of handedness, with a moderate increase in compensatory movements.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp2.

claim: Exp3 tested the control on seven participants with unilateral transhumeral limb loss, three of them disabled on their left side.
source: As we now have an intuitive control applicable to participants with an arm amputation on either side of their body, we tested it on seven participants with unilateral transhumeral limb loss, three of them disabled on their left side.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, no initial acquisition phase was conducted on participants with limb loss.
source: As no initial acquisition phase was conducted on these participants, the set of 200 possible targets was determined for each of them using a self-organizing map to extract representative postures from a large number of postures generated by movements produced by all participants of Exp1 filtered to the range of motion of their residual limb (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, two blocks of intuitive control with the Generic ANN were conducted on participants' amputated side before they were tested on the same mirrored targets with their valid arm.
source: Therefore, two blocks of intuitive control with the Generic ANN were conducted on their amputated side (TestGeneric 1 and 2, Figure 3), before they were tested on the same mirrored targets with their valid arm (TestNat).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, all median success rates were above 99%.
source: As for other experiments, success rates were very high (all medians above 99%), and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 99.24% vs 99.50% vs 99.50%, respectively, n=1128; Cochran's Q test, p=0.1146, Q=4.33, df = 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, success rates did not differ between conditions (p=0.1146).
source: As for other experiments, success rates were very high (all medians above 99%), and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 99.24% vs 99.50% vs 99.50%, respectively, n=1128; Cochran's Q test, p=0.1146, Q=4.33, df = 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, median movement times were 1.27 s for TestGeneric1, 1.16 s for TestGeneric2, and 1.40 s for TestNat.
source: Movement times with our movement-based control were also in the same range as in previous experiments, and were even smaller by the second block of intuitive control (TestGeneric2) than with their valid arm (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 1.27 s vs 1.16 s vs 1.40 s; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.002, chi-squared=12.286, df = 2; post-hoc Conover test; TestGeneric1 vs TestNat, p=0.619; TestGeneric2 vs TestNat, p=0.014; TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2, p=0.161).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, movement times for TestGeneric2 were significantly smaller than for TestNat (p=0.014).
source: Movement times with our movement-based control were also in the same range as in previous experiments, and were even smaller by the second block of intuitive control (TestGeneric2) than with their valid arm (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 1.27 s vs 1.16 s vs 1.40 s; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.002, chi-squared=12.286, df = 2; post-hoc Conover test; TestGeneric1 vs TestNat, p=0.619; TestGeneric2 vs TestNat, p=0.014; TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2, p=0.161).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, median shoulder volumes were 0.36 dm³ for TestGeneric1, 0.37 dm³ for TestGeneric2, and 0.33 dm³ for TestNat.
source: The volumes spread by the shoulder were comparable to that measured with the generic model on Exp2 (median 0.43 dm3) and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 0.36 dm3 vs 0.37 dm3 vs 0.33 dm3; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.867, chi-squared=0.28571, df = 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Exp3.

claim: In Exp3, shoulder volumes did not differ between conditions (p=0.867).
source: The volumes spread by the shoulder were comparable to that measured with the generic model on Exp2 (median 0.43 dm3) and did not differ between conditions (TestGeneric1 vs TestGeneric2 vs TestNat; medians of 0.36 dm3 vs 0.37 dm3 vs 0.33 dm3; n=7; Friedman test, p=0.867, chi-squared=0.28571, df = 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Exp3.

claim: Without any prior experience with the task nor with the apparatus, the intuitive control allowed disabled participants to achieve performance as good as with their valid arm.
source: Overall, without any prior experience with the task nor with the apparatus, our intuitive control allowed disabled participants to achieve performance as good as with their valid arm, and to achieve comparable levels of performance as for other subjects in all conditions tested (see Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Exp3.

claim: The intuitive control elicited high enthusiasm from participants with limb loss.
source: Furthermore, beyond objective performance measures, our intuitive control elicited high enthusiasm from participants with limb loss.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from Exp3.

source: Participant 1: 'A prosthesis that would be controlled like that? I take it right away.'

source: Participant2: 'At the end, it is quite intuitive.'
evidence: This is a direct quote from a participant.

source: Participant 3 reported that he would use a prosthesis behaving like this.

source: Participant 4: 'Doing a real arm movement, this is enjoyable.'

claim: A Proof of Concept was conducted whereby 15 participants, including two with acquired and one with congenital transhumeral limb difference, were involved in reaching and grasping real objects.
source: To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in the physical world, we conducted a Proof of Concept (POC) whereby 15 participants, including two with acquired and one with congenital transhumeral limb difference, were involved in reaching and grasping real objects in various positions and orientations with our novel control applied on a humanoid robotic platform specifically designed to explore human-robot control strategies (Mick et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the physical proof of concept experiment.

claim: In the physical POC, the shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the robotic arm were operated from real shoulder movement produced by the operator.
source: As with the Hybrid Arm used to emulate the behavior of an upper arm fitted with a transhumeral prosthesis in virtual reality (Figure 1e), the shoulder flexion-extension and abduction-adduction of the robotic arm were operated from real shoulder movement produced by the operator, whereas the five remaining distal joint angles were driven by prediction from the generic ANN (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes the control scheme for the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator.
source: In contrast to virtual reality, however, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator, such that compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
evidence: This describes a key difference in the physical POC setup.

claim: In the physical POC, compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
source: In contrast to virtual reality, however, the torso of the humanoid robotic platform was fixed and independent of the operator, such that compensatory movements from the trunk and from shoulder translations were not transmitted to the device.
evidence: This describes a key difference in the physical POC setup.

claim: In the physical POC, high success rates were achieved by all participants in both conditions.
source: Despite the functionality of compensatory movement being withdrawn by design, high success rates were achieved by all participants in both conditions (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a qualitative result from the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, median success rates were 93% for TestGeneric and 100% for TestNat.
source: A significant difference was nevertheless found between the proportion of validated targets using our movement-base control and natural control (TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 93% vs 100%, respectively; n=180; McNemar test, p=0.0003, chi.sq=13.1, df = 1; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, there was a significant difference in success rate between TestGeneric and TestNat (p=0.0003).
source: A significant difference was nevertheless found between the proportion of validated targets using our movement-base control and natural control (TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 93% vs 100%, respectively; n=180; McNemar test, p=0.0003, chi.sq=13.1, df = 1; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, the congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (14/15).
source: The congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (i.e. 14/15), and the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets which means that only one target was failed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result for a specific participant in the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets.
source: The congenital limb different participant was able to reach and grasp 93.3% of the targets (i.e. 14/15), and the two participants with transhumeral limb loss were both able to grasp 80% of the first five targets which means that only one target was failed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result for specific participants in the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm.
source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, median movement times were 6.08 s for TestGeneric and 5.98 s for TestNat.
source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the physical POC.

claim: In the physical POC, there was no significant difference in movement times between TestGeneric and TestNat (p=0.7026).
source: Furthermore, the validated targets were reached and grasped with movement times similar to those obtained using natural control applied to the robotic arm (POCa-b TestGeneric vs TestNat; medians 6.08 s vs 5.98 s, respectively; two-tailed paired t-test, p=0.7026, t=–0.39198, df = 11; Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the physical POC.

claim: The first feature that enabled the movement-based control to work well was to introduce the movement goal as an input to the trained ANN.
source: The first feature that enabled our movement-based control to work so well compared to previous attempts was to introduce the movement goal as an input to the trained ANN.
evidence: This is stated as a critical feature of the approach.

claim: Without movement goal as input, the ANN would predict the most likely configuration of the distal joints for a given proximal posture, but irrespective of the location of the object to reach.
source: Without it, the ANN would predict the most likely configuration of the distal joints for a given proximal (shoulder) posture, but irrespective of the location of the object to reach.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous approaches.

claim: The workspace was greatly expanded by starting from the widest possible workspace, limited by the maximal range of motion of participants.
source: First, we greatly expanded the applicable workspace of this control. This was achieved by starting from the widest possible workspace, limited by the maximal range of motion of participants, and subsequently using a self-organizing network (Fritzke, 1994) to best represent the space covered by participants while producing natural arm movements within this space.
evidence: This describes a methodological improvement.

claim: The amount of relevant training data was substantially increased by using the entire trajectories of the recorded natural arm movements.
source: Second, we substantially increased the amount of relevant training data, by using the entire trajectories of the recorded natural arm movements, instead of using only arm postures placing the hand sufficiently close to the target (Mick et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a methodological improvement.

claim: The use of entire trajectories was made efficient by artificially placing the target in the hand.
source: Critically, the use of the entire trajectories was made efficient by artificially placing the target in the hand (see Methods), such that the ANN trained on those data performs a form of natural inverse kinematic solving, i.e., one that provides a solution that is representative of natural arm postures rather than a mere optimization for an arbitrary cost function.
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation.

claim: The control was made applicable to people with limb loss by transferring humeral rotation as an output of the ANN.
source: Here, the humeral rotation was transferred as an output of the ANN, being a predicted output rather than a necessary input for the control system.
evidence: This describes a methodological change to enable applicability to people with limb loss.

claim: A generic control was designed based on natural movements from multiple other individuals, but specifically tuned to the morphology of the user.
source: In addition, instead of training the control on natural arm movements specifically produced by the intended user (also not applicable in people with limb loss), we designed a generic control based on natural movements from multiple other individuals, but specifically tuned to the morphology of the user (see Methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach for the Generic ANN.

claim: Specific tuning to the morphology of the user was essential, since a given target position and orientation could call for markedly different arm postures depending on the particular arm morphology of an intended user.
source: This specific tuning was essential, since a given target position and orientation could call for markedly different arm postures depending on the particular arm morphology of an intended user.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the morphology-specific tuning.

claim: Mirror symmetry with respect to the medial plane was applied to accommodate for either side of an amputation.
source: Finally, mirror symmetry with respect to the medial plane was applied to accommodate for either side of an amputation.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to handle different amputation sides.

claim: Including movement goal as an input of the control system could be seen as a weakness, as it might be difficult to determine in real-life settings.
source: Despite the clear benefits mentioned above, including movement goal as an input of the control system could be seen as a weakness, as it might be difficult to determine in real-life settings.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation.

claim: Impressive progress in artificial intelligence and computer vision makes determining movement goals appear well within grasp.
source: Yet, impressive progress in artificial intelligence and computer vision is such that what would have been difficult to imagine a decade ago appears now well within grasp (LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited as a reason why the limitation may be overcome.

claim: Deep learning combined with gaze information enables identifying an object that is about to be grasped from an egocentric view on glasses.
source: For instance, we showed recently that deep learning combined with gaze information enables identifying an object that is about to be grasped from an egocentric view on glasses (Pérez de San Roman et al., 2017), and this even in complex cluttered natural environments (González-Díaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited as evidence that movement goals can be determined.

claim: Six-dimensional object pose estimation is a very active area of computer vision.
source: Six-dimensional object pose estimation is also a very active area of computer vision (Liu, 2022; Nguyen et al., 2022), and prosthesis control strategies based on computer vision combined with gaze and/or myoelectric control for movement intention detection are quickly developing (Starke et al., 2022; Markovic et al., 2015; Krausz et al., 2020; Ghazaei et al., 2017; Mouchoux et al., 2021; He et al., 2020), illustrating the promises of this approach.
evidence: This is cited as evidence of progress in relevant technologies.

claim: Generalizing the approach to multiple tasks including more constrained reaches will require future work.
source: It remains that generalizing our approach to multiple tasks including more constrained reaches will require future work.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation requiring future work.

claim: Further developments are needed to produce natural trajectories compatible with real-world applications.
source: Although our approach enabled participants to converge to the correct position and orientation to grasp simple objects with movement times similar to those of natural movements, it is important to note that further developments are needed to produce natural trajectories compatible with real-world applications.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation requiring future work.

claim: The distal joints predicted by the ANN are realized instantaneously such that a discontinuity occurs at each target change.
source: As easily visible in Videos 2–4, the distal joints predicted by the ANN are realized instantaneously such that a discontinuity occurs at each target change, whereby the distal part of the arm jumps to the novel prediction associated with the new target location.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation of the approach.

claim: A requirement for the control to be functional on a prosthesis is to have actuated wrist joints available.
source: Another requirement for our control to be functional on a prosthesis is to have actuated wrist joints available, as those are essential to orient the hand in space (Montagnani et al., 2015a; Kanitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for practical implementation.

claim: Most commercial prostheses do not have actuated wrist joints.
source: This is not the case for most commercial prostheses, which sometimes include wrist flexion-extension (mostly passive), and very rarely wrist radial-ulnar deviation (Bajaj et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited as a limitation of current commercial prostheses.

claim: The LUKE/DEKA arm includes two wrist degrees of freedom as actuated joints.
source: Notable exceptions include the LUKE/DEKA arm (Resnik et al., 2014a) and the RIC arm (Lenzi et al., 2016), which both include those two degrees of freedom as actuated joints, but with a fixed linear relationship between them.
evidence: This is cited as an exception to the limitation of commercial prostheses.

claim: The RIC arm includes two wrist degrees of freedom as actuated joints.
source: Notable exceptions include the LUKE/DEKA arm (Resnik et al., 2014a) and the RIC arm (Lenzi et al., 2016), which both include those two degrees of freedom as actuated joints, but with a fixed linear relationship between them.
evidence: This is cited as an exception to the limitation of commercial prostheses.

claim: The solution proposed is suitable to control distal arm joints to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects in a wide workspace, but not for fine hand and grasp control involved in object manipulations.
source: As already mentioned, the solution proposed here is suitable to control distal arm joints to place the hand at a correct position and orientation to grasp objects in a wide workspace, but not for fine hand and grasp control involved in object manipulations, which relies heavily on tactile and somatosensory feedback information (Marasco et al., 2021; Marasco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a scope limitation of the proposed solution.

claim: The movement-based approach appears complementary to more invasive ones, which specifically target hand and grasp functions through bi-directional interactions with the nervous system.
source: In this context, our movement-based approach appears complementary to more invasive ones, which specifically target those latter functions through bi-directional interactions with the nervous system for both motor control and sensory processing (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a; D'Anna et al., 2019; Zollo et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a potential integration with other approaches.

claim: Combining the movement-based approach with osseointegration at humeral level would restore amplitude and control over shoulder movements.
source: Combining those with osseointegration at humeral level (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2020; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014a) would be particularly relevant as this would also restore amplitude and control over shoulder movements, which are essential for our control but greatly affected by conventional residual limb fitting harnesses and sockets.
evidence: This is stated as a potential beneficial combination.

claim: The movement-based approach could be combined with semi-autonomous grasp control to accommodate for multiple grasp functions.
source: Finally, our movement-based approach could also be combined with semi-autonomous grasp control to accommodate for multiple grasp functions (Starke et al., 2022; Ghazaei et al., 2017; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a potential integration with other approaches.

claim: The control could be used as is in virtual reality for the management of Phantom-Limb Pain.
source: Besides developments needed for application to a real-life setting, the control proposed here could be used as is in virtual reality for the management of Phantom-Limb Pain (PLP), a painful sensation perceived in the missing limb that often occurs after an amputation.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application.

claim: Reduction of pain has been repeatedly reported using mirror therapy.
source: Although the precise mechanisms behind PLP and its proposed treatments are still debated and unresolved (Di Pino et al., 2021; Makin and Flor, 2020), reduction of pain has been repeatedly reported using mirror therapy, whereby the intact hand is moved while the patient views it through a mirror at the place of his/her missing limb (Chan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited as evidence for a treatment approach.

claim: Mirror therapy was found ineffective on patients with distorted (telescoped) phantom limb.
source: Yet, mirror therapy was found ineffective on patients with distorted (telescoped) phantom limb (Foell et al., 2014), and is not applicable to people with bilateral limb loss.
evidence: This is cited as a limitation of mirror therapy.

claim: Mirror therapy is not applicable to people with bilateral limb loss.
source: Yet, mirror therapy was found ineffective on patients with distorted (telescoped) phantom limb (Foell et al., 2014), and is not applicable to people with bilateral limb loss.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of mirror therapy.

claim: The limitations of mirror therapy can be overcome in virtual reality.
source: Those two limitations can easily be overcome in virtual reality (Thøgersen et al., 2020), and our novel movement-based control provides a solution immediately available to control virtual (missing) limbs with natural coordination solely from residual limb motion.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the proposed approach.

claim: Self-reported feedback from amputated participants indicates that overall, they found the prosthesis control solution intuitive and natural.
source: Importantly, self-reported feedback from amputated participants indicates that overall, they found our prosthesis control solution intuitive and natural, and would use it should it be available on their prosthesis (see Results, Successful validation on individuals with limb loss).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of participant feedback.

source: Exp1 was conducted on 10 naive, intact-limbs, right-handed participants (five males, EHI mean 84.0; SD 18.4), aged 24–43 years (mean 27.3; SD 6.0).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Exp1.

source: Exp2 was conducted on 12 naive, intact-limbs participants (eight males), aged 20–35 years (mean 24.1; SD 4.4).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Exp2.

claim: Exp3 was conducted on seven naive participants having undergone transhumeral amputation (seven males), aged 25–48 (mean 40.4; SD 8.4).
source: Exp3 was conducted on seven naive participants having undergone transhumeral amputation ( seven males), aged 25–48 (mean 40.4; SD 8.4).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Exp3.

claim: POCa-b was conducted on 12 naive, intact-limbs participants (six males, EHI mean 87.1; SD 22.8), aged 19–69 years (mean 33.3; SD 16.6).
source: POCa-b was conducted on 12 naive, intact-limbs participants (six males, EHI mean 87.1; SD 22.8), aged 19–69 years (mean 33.3; SD 16.6).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for POCa-b.

claim: POCc was conducted on one congenital limb different participant, with forearm malformation on the right side, male, aged 22, naive about the task.
source: POCc was conducted on one congenital limb different participant, with forearm malformation on the right side, male, aged 22, naive about the task.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for POCc.

source: POCd was conducted on two male participants who had undergone transhumeral amputation on the right side, aged 34 and 39 years.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for POCd.

claim: All participants gave their informed consent.
source: All participants gave their informed consent and the research presented here has been conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with a local ethics committee (CCP Est II: n°2019-A02890-57).
evidence: This is stated as an ethical compliance measure.

claim: The research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with a local ethics committee (CCP Est II: n°2019-A02890-57).
source: All participants gave their informed consent and the research presented here has been conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with a local ethics committee (CCP Est II: n°2019-A02890-57).
evidence: This is stated as an ethical compliance measure.

claim: The virtual arm skeleton consisted of three rigid segments (upper arm, forearm, and hand) linked to each other by spherical joints.
source: The scene displayed a virtual arm whose skeleton consisted of three rigid segments (upper arm, forearm, and hand) linked to each other by spherical joints.
evidence: This describes the virtual arm model used.

claim: The network structure includes two densely connected layers of 256 neurons each, a dropout layer with a drop fraction of 0.5, and a dense layer of 64 neurons.
source: The network structure includes two densely connected layers of 256 neurons each, a dropout layer with a drop fraction of 0.5, and a dense layer of 64 neurons.
evidence: This describes the ANN architecture used.

claim: The network was implemented and trained using TensorFlow in association with Keras as the programming interface.
source: The network was implemented and trained using TensorFlow in association with Keras as the programming interface.
evidence: This describes the software tools used for implementation.

claim: Thirty epochs were done with a learning rate of 1e-4 for the Own ANN.
source: Thirty epochs were done with a learning rate of 1e-4, similar to that used in Mick et al., 2021.
evidence: This describes the training parameters for the Own ANN.

claim: For the Generic ANN, the epoch number was reduced to 10 to minimize computation time.
source: However, the training dataset included data from 10 participants instead of just one, thus containing approximately 10 times more samples than data used to train an Own ANN. Given this, the epoch number was reduced to 10 to minimize computation time, and a momentum parameter was introduced to further prevent overfitting.
evidence: This describes the training parameters for the Generic ANN.

claim: A learning rate of 1.59e-7 combined with a momentum of 0.95 constitutes a good compromise for the Generic ANN.
source: An offline analysis indicated that a learning rate of 1.59e-7 combined with a momentum of 0.95 constitutes a good compromise for the Generic ANN to perform well both when the target is considered in the hand (as for the training data used) and when moving toward it (as it is mostly the case during online experimental phases).
evidence: This describes the optimized training parameters for the Generic ANN.

claim: A hard constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 2 cm and an angular tolerance of 5°.
source: A hard constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 2 cm and an angular tolerance of 5°, whereas a relaxed constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 4 cm and an angular tolerance of 10°.
evidence: This describes the task constraints used.

claim: A relaxed constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 4 cm and an angular tolerance of 10°.
source: A hard constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 2 cm and an angular tolerance of 5°, whereas a relaxed constraint was defined with a spatial tolerance of 4 cm and an angular tolerance of 10°.
evidence: This describes the task constraints used.

claim: Data were first filtered to remove trials with substantial measurement errors associated with motion capture.
source: Data were first filtered to remove trials with substantial measurement errors associated with motion capture.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing approach.

claim: Over all experiments, the filtering process removed an average of 3.8 (±7.6) % trials per participant and experimental phase.
source: Over all experiments, this process removed an average of 3.8 (±7.6) % trials per participant and experimental phase.
evidence: This is a quantitative result of the data filtering process.
